exam: A 12‑year‑old presents with fever, bruising, and WBC 80 × 10⁹/L – what immediate investigation and why? — Peripheral smear to look for blasts and assess leukostasis risk.
How would you differentiate AML from ALL on a smear? — Look for Auer rods (AML) and assess nuclear‑cytoplasmic ratio; confirm with flow cytometry.
A patient with known HIV develops pancytopenia – what red‑flag features suggest acute leukemia? — Presence of blasts, rapid drop in counts, and systemic symptoms.
What are the indications for leukapheresis in acute leukemia? — Hyperleukocytosis >100 × 10⁹/L with neurological or respiratory compromise.
Why is allopurinol preferred over rasburicase in most low‑resource settings? — Allopurinol is inexpensive, oral, and widely available; rasburicase requires refrigeration.
Explain why anthracyclines are contraindicated in a patient with prior myocardial infarction. — They cause dose‑dependent cardiotoxicity that can worsen existing cardiac damage.
What supportive measures reduce early mortality in acute leukemia? — Prompt antibiotics, transfusion of red cells/platelets, hydration, and tumor‑lysis prophylaxis.
How does co‑existing malaria affect the presentation of acute leukemia? — Malaria can cause anemia and thrombocytopenia, masking marrow failure and delaying diagnosis.
ai.title: Acute Leukemia
ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: Acute leukemia is a rapid proliferation of immature white blood cells that replaces normal marrow, causing cytopenias and systemic symptoms. Prompt recognition, basic labs, and urgent referral are essential, especially where diagnostics are limited.

b: Rapid onset of fatigue, fever, bruising
Pancytopenia on CBC
High blast percentage (≥20%) on peripheral smear
sections.p: Acute leukemia presents with marrow failure and infiltration of blasts into blood and organs. Two main subtypes are lymphoid (ALL) and myeloid (AML). In low‑resource settings, infections and malnutrition often modify presentation.

b: Morphology: Auer rods suggest AML
TdT positivity points to ALL
Cytogenetics (e.g., t(9;22), MLL rearrangement) guide prognosis
sections.p: Diagnosis requires confirming ≥20% blasts in blood or marrow, classifying lineage by morphology and immunophenotype, and assessing risk with cytogenetics when available.

b: Infection risk: neutropenia + mucosal breach
Bleeding: thrombocytopenia, DIC in AML M3
Hyperleukocytosis: risk of leukostasis (neurologic, respiratory)
sections.p: Patients often present with infections, bleeding, or organ infiltration. In East Africa, co‑existing HIV, malaria, or TB can mask or worsen cytopenias.

t.b: Is there marrow failure? – Low Hb, low platelets, neutropenia; blasts raise WBC
What cells are present? – Morphology identifies blasts, Auer rods, lymphoblast features
Confirm diagnosis and % blasts – ≥20% blasts confirms acute leukemia
Which lineage? – CD34, CD19, CD10 for ALL; CD13, CD33, MPO for AML
Prognostic risk – Detect t(9;22), MLL, FLT3; if unavailable, use clinical risk factors
Is tumor lysis imminent? – High uric acid/LDH signals need prophylaxis

b: Broad‑spectrum antibiotics for febrile neutropenia
Allogenic or autologous blood transfusion for symptomatic anemia or bleeding
Allopurinol or rasburicase (if available) for tumor‑lysis prophylaxis
Hydration and diuretics to maintain urine output
Urgent referral to a centre with chemotherapy capability
sections.p: Start supportive care immediately, then refer for definitive chemotherapy. In low‑resource hospitals, focus on infection control, transfusion, and tumor‑lysis prophylaxis.

b: Aplastic anemia: pancytopenia but no blasts
Severe sepsis: fever and leukocytosis but blasts absent
Myelodysplastic syndrome: <20% blasts, chronic course
sections.p: Acute leukemia can mimic severe infection, aplastic anemia, or myelodysplastic syndrome.

b: Low blast count in blood does not exclude marrow disease
High WBC can be leukemoid reaction; look for immature morphology
sections.p: Peripheral smear may show few blasts early; marrow may be hypocellular in early disease, giving a false‑negative impression.

b: Identify leukostasis signs (dyspnea, neurological deficits) and need for urgent cytoreduction
Explain why anthracyclines are avoided in severe cardiac disease
Discuss impact of HIV on prognosis and treatment choice
sections.p: Examiners test ability to prioritize investigations, recognise emergencies, and understand treatment principles without memorising drug doses.

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden neurological change or respiratory distress (leukostasis)
